+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 52.2
Prompt:
Cozy spacepunk The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The Last Outpost hums with the low buzz of conversation, punctuated by the clinks of glasses and the whir of the ventilation system. The lights are dim, casting a warm glow on the eclectic decor—vintage holo-ads flickering on the walls, mismatched bar stools, and a collection of trinkets from different worlds hanging from the ceiling like curious stars. I wipe the same spot on the bar counter for the fifth time, though it’s already spotless. It's a habit I can't shake; a need to keep my hands busy while I listen. “Hey, Nets!” a familiar voice calls from the far end of the bar. It’s Taro, a miner with a penchant for tall tales and a knack for getting into trouble. “You got any of that spiced rum left, or did you sell it all to the last crew that came through?” I glance up, my rag still in hand. “You know I always save a bottle for you, Taro. Just don’t spill it on my floor again, alright? I’m still scrubbing out that last batch of your ‘accident.’” He chuckles, a deep, rumbling sound that reminds me of the asteroid fields outside. “You’re a saint, Nets. I swear I’ll pay you back one of these days.” “Sure you will,” I reply, rolling my eyes, but I’m smiling. I pour him a generous glass, and as I set it down, I catch sight of the stranger at the bar. He’s a mess—tentacled dreads hanging wildly from his head, his skin a deep shade of blue that glimmers under the lights. He slumps over the bar, looking like the weight of the universe rests on his shoulders. I lean in a bit closer, curiosity piquing my interest. “You look like you could use a drink,” I say, trying to keep my tone light. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double,” he replies, barely glancing my way. His voice is rough, like gravel scraping against metal. “Coming right up,” I say, pouring the amber liquid into a glass. I slide it over to him, watching as he downs half of it in one swift motion. He winces but doesn’t say anything. I wipe the counter again, feeling the need to fill the silence. “Rough day?” He looks up finally, his eyes a stormy mix of emotions I can’t quite place. “You could say that.” He takes another gulp, then leans back, his gaze drifting toward the wall. “More like a rough life.” I nod, trying to gauge his mood. “Out here in the belt, it’s easy to feel lost. You from around here?” “Not even close,” he says, his tentacles twitching slightly. “I’m just passing through. Got mixed up with the wrong crowd. Thought I could outrun them.” I set my rag down and lean a little closer, intrigued. “Sounds like a story worth telling. I’m all ears.” He lets out a short laugh, though it’s laced with bitterness. “Yeah, well, it’s not a pretty one. My name’s Zarek, by the way.” “Nettle, but most call me Nets.” I extend my hand, and he takes it, his grip firm but unsteady. “So, what kind of trouble are we talking about?” Zarek hesitates, the weight of his thoughts palpable in the air. “You ever hear of the Red Cartel?” I feel my stomach drop at the mention of the name. The Red Cartel is notorious around these parts—smugglers, thieves, and worse. “Yeah, I’ve heard of them. Why?” He sighs, his shoulders slumping further. “I owe them… a lot. More than I can pay back. They’re not the forgiving type, you know?” I wipe the counter again, though I’m not really cleaning anymore. “And you think they’ll come looking for you here?” “Isn’t that what cartels do?” He smirks, but it doesn’t reach his eyes. “I thought I could lay low for a bit, get my bearings, but I don’t know how long I can hide.” “Zarek,” I say, leaning in closer, “you can’t stay here if they’re after you. They’ll tear this place apart.” He shakes his head, staring into his glass like it holds the answers. “What am I supposed to do? I’ve got nowhere else to go. I thought I was free when I left, but they always find you, don’t they?” “Not if you stay smart,” I reply, trying to sound more confident than I feel. “You could leave the Outpost—there are plenty of ships heading out, and you could get lost in the expanse.” He finally meets my gaze, and for a moment, I see a flicker of hope in his eyes. “You really think I could just… leave?” “Why not?” I say, shrugging. “You’ve got skills, right? You can barter, negotiate. You’re a survivor.” “Survivor,” he repeats, a bitter laugh escaping his lips. “That’s a nice way to put it. More like a coward who runs away.” I can’t help but feel a pang of empathy for him. I know what it’s like to run from your past, to hide in plain sight. “Sometimes running is the only option,” I say softly. “But you need a plan. You can’t just sit here and wait for them to find you.” Zarek leans back in his chair, his eyes narrowing as he considers my words. “What do you know about plans? You’re just a bartender.” “Yeah, but I’ve seen a lot of things from behind this bar,” I reply, crossing my arms. “I’ve seen what happens when people don’t act. You don’t want to end up like them.” He studies me for a moment, and I can’t shake the feeling that he’s weighing my words against whatever demons are chasing him. “And what if I don’t want to run? What if I want to face them?” “Then you better be ready,” I say, my voice firm. “Because they won’t go easy on you. They’ll come for you, and they won’t stop until they get what they want.” Zarek’s gaze hardens, determination flickering in his eyes. “Then I guess I better start preparing.” “Just remember,” I warn, wiping the bar again, “the Last Outpost may feel safe, but it’s only as secure as the people who walk through its doors. Don’t let your past come crashing in.” He nods, but I can see the storm brewing behind his eyes. I don’t know what he’ll decide, but I know one thing for certain: this is only the beginning.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is competent, professional-feeling prose that follows the basic instructions: first person, present tense, conflict established (Zarek's debt to the Red Cartel) and unresolved, roughly dialogue-heavy (probably around 60-65% dialogue). However, it's generic. The opening scene-setting is stock cozy-bar description with little specificity that earns the "spacepunk" or "Andromeda outer rim" flavor. Character names like Taro and Zarek, and the "Red Cartel," are boilerplate space-opera furniture. The dialogue is functional but weak: characters state feelings directly ("I owe them… a lot," "I thought I could outrun them"), and Nets repeatedly asks questions that pull exposition out of the stranger like a script. Nets' backstory ("escaping from her past life") is touched only glancingly ("I know what it's like to run") — a tell, not a show. The stranger's emotional arc within one conversation — from despair to "determination flickering in his eyes" and deciding to "start preparing" — is too fast and unearned. Repetitive tics ("wiping the counter again," "flicker of hope/determination in his eyes," "storm behind his eyes") undercut the prose quality. The line "this is only the beginning" is a cliched close. Nets' character voice is consistent but thin; she's a generic wise bartender. The emotion is stated rather than evoked. Coherence is fine, pacing is adequate, no purple prose, no meandering to speak of. It's a serviceable chapter that lacks surprise, specificity, and depth. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 49.1
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Chapter Two: Ground Zero The strap on my backpack keeps slipping off my shoulder, and it’s starting to drive me insane. I swear, I tug it back up every five seconds, but it’s like the damn thing has a mind of its own. Maybe it's trying to escape too. I mean, I guess I can’t blame it. Who wants to be stuck with a runaway like me in a city that smells like beignets and desperation? New Orleans. The name alone used to send a thrill through me, a promise of jazz and freedom. But now, standing on a cracked sidewalk in the French Quarter, I feel like I’m lost in a postcard. The colors are vibrant, the music is chaotic, and I’m just… here, standing still, a ghost among the living. I take a deep breath and try to focus. My heart’s racing, not just from the sheer excitement of being here, but also from the panic of being alone. I can’t go back. I won’t. But I don’t know where to go next. My phone’s dead—no charger, no plan—so I’m basically a walking “lost and found” sign. “Hey! You okay?” A voice pulls me from my thoughts. I turn to see a girl about my age, maybe a year or two older, leaning against a lamppost. She’s wearing a faded band tee and ripped jeans, her dark hair falling in messy waves around her face. There’s a certain fire in her eyes that flickers with interest, and for a moment, I think maybe she sees me. “Um, yeah,” I stammer, trying to sound casual. “Just… taking it all in.” “Right.” She raises an eyebrow, not buying it for a second. “You look like you just stepped off the set of a coming-of-age film. Where’s your crew?” I can’t help but let out a laugh, half nervous, half genuine. “No crew. Just me. Just… got here.” “Nice. I’m Roxy.” She pushes off the lamppost and walks closer, her hands shoved deep into her pockets. “You must be new to the runaway scene.” “Runaway scene?” I echo, feeling a bit dumb. I mean, I know what I am, but the way she says it makes it sound almost like… a community. “Yeah, you know. The streets, the parks, the occasional dumpster dive for food.” She gestures around. “It’s not all bad, if you know where to look. Want a coffee? Or, like, a beignet? I promise they’re worth it.” Coffee sounds good, but I don’t have any money. I’m about to say no when she shrugs, her expression unreadable but inviting. “I got you. Just don’t drink it all at once. It’s potent around here.” “Thanks,” I mumble, feeling a flicker of warmth in my chest. For a moment, I forget about my family, my past, the chaos of the last two days. I just focus on Roxy, who seems to be a lifeline, however thin. As we walk, the sounds of the city swirl around us—jazz musicians playing on street corners, the chatter of tourists, the sweet scent of fried dough. It’s intoxicating, but I can’t shake the feeling that I’m an outsider looking in. “So, what’s your story?” Roxy asks, casually sipping her coffee as we reach a small café. “You don’t look like someone who just decided to go on a spontaneous road trip.” I hesitate, the weight of my truth heavy on my tongue. “I—uh, I had to leave home. Family stuff. Just… needed to be me, you know?” She nods slowly, her gaze steady. “I get it. Family can be a real trip sometimes. What about friends? Anyone you’re missing?” “No friends,” I admit, the words tasting bitter. “Just me. I thought it’d be easier… but I feel kinda lost.” “Welcome to the club,” Roxy says with a half-smile. “I’ve been there too. You’re not alone in this, even if it feels like it.” She leans in slightly, lowering her voice. “But you gotta be careful. This city has its dangers, even if the music makes you forget for a minute.” “I know,” I reply, the reminder pulling me back to reality. “I just… didn’t think about that.” We sit down at a small table outside the café, and Roxy pulls out a half-eaten beignet from her bag, offering me a piece. I take it, the sugary sweetness melting in my mouth, a moment of pure bliss. “So, where are you staying?” she asks. I look down at my hands, the reality of my situation crashing in like cold water. “I don’t really have a place. Just… wandering.” “Wandering can be fun, but it’s safer with a plan,” she says, her tone softening. “You could crash with me for a night or two. Just until you figure things out.” Part of me wants to shout ‘yes!’ because, honestly, the thought of sleeping on a bench again makes my stomach churn. But another part of me is screaming to hold back. “What’s the catch?” Roxy laughs lightly, a sound that’s both refreshing and disarming. “No catch. Just don’t expect me to babysit you. I’ve got my own issues, and I’m not exactly a responsible adult.” I chuckle, the tension in my shoulders easing a bit. “I can handle that.” “Good. Let’s see what this place has to offer, then.” She stands up, offering her hand. “Welcome to New Orleans, Taylor. Let’s make some memories that don’t suck.” As I take her hand and stand up, I can’t help but feel a strange sense of hope. Maybe I’m not just a runaway. Maybe, just maybe, I’m on the brink of something new.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter hits the basic structural requirements: first person, Taylor's voice, a first day in New Orleans, a runaway encounter (Roxy), some internal monologue, and roughly the requested length. Beyond that, it's a fairly generic, safe execution of a prompt that asked for intensity and conflict. Strengths: The voice is consistent and readable, with a wry, self-deprecating teen tone ("a walking 'lost and found' sign"). The prose flows adequately, sentences are clear, and the pacing is brisk. The setting details (beignets, street jazz, French Quarter) are present but stock postcard-level. Weaknesses: The prompt demanded a teen "grappling with intense & conflicting emotions" after a catastrophic coming-out and impulsive flight. The response sandboxes this almost immediately. Taylor's trans identity and family disaster are reduced to "family stuff... needed to be me" — a single vague gesture — and the panic of the first 48 hours evaporates within paragraphs. The emotional register is muted, more quirky-indie-film than desperate runaway. Roxy is meant to be "a runaway with issues and secrets," but she's transparently friendly, instantly generous, and reveals nothing. There's no tension, no ambiguity, no sense of danger — the prompt's "not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are" is addressed with one line of Roxy saying "this city has its dangers" and then a full offer of a place to stay within minutes of meeting. Taylor's guardedness is stated ("another part of me is screaming to hold back") rather than dramatized, and then dissolves in a handshake. The dialogue is serviceable but cliché ("Welcome to the club," "Let's make some memories that don't suck"), and the ending lands on unearned uplift: hope, a new friend, a fresh start — all achieved without cost, risk, or emotional work. The mixed-tense instruction is only half-honored; the piece is almost uniformly past tense. The "runaway scene" framing is a mildly interesting idea but underdeveloped. Overall: competent, coherent, mildly pleasant, but shallow. It reads like a writing exercise rather than a lived chapter. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 51.6
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** Midas scratched his chin thoughtfully, or rather, he attempted to scratch it through the grizzled beard he hadn’t bothered to trim since the Great Collapse of Technology. It was a remarkably unimpressive beard, being neither bushy nor well-groomed, just a scraggly assortment of wiry hair that had taken on a life of its own, much like the world outside. “Today,” he said, addressing his only companion in the dimness of their makeshift den, “we need to find food. Actual food, not just the last remnants of expired canned beans. I’m thinking…fruit. Or perhaps a vegetable that hasn’t turned into a science experiment.” Chewy, his animo-tronic stuffed koala, perched upon a half-melted stool, tilted his head in what could only be described as an endearing manner. The koala’s button eyes gleamed with an odd mix of wisdom and mischief, and he emitted a low, mechanical whirr as his voice crackled to life. “Give ’em the ol’ one-two! Fresh is best, but frozen is fine!” Chewy blurted out, his voice sounding like a malfunctioning radio tuned to a station that hadn’t broadcast since the days when everyone had their own food delivery drones. Midas sighed, wondering if he’d have to explain advertising slogans to a stuffed animal one day. “Right. Frozen food it is. Because, you know, we live in a post-apocalyptic world where freezing things is still a thing,” Midas said dryly, as he rummaged through his meager supply of scavenged clothing. He pulled on a pair of trousers with a suspicious stain that he chose to ignore and a shirt with a logo that he no longer understood, but it seemed to fit the theme of his current existence: “Prevail with Peas.” With Chewy bouncing awkwardly under his arm, they set off into the outside world, which had once been a bustling city but now resembled a nature documentary narrated by a particularly snarky David Attenborough. Vines hung from crumbling buildings like green snakes, and the streets were littered with debris that had accumulated over the years: old smartphones, broken bicycles, and the occasional wind-up toy that still twitched sporadically. “Let’s head towards the market,” Midas suggested, pointing in the vague direction of what used to be a supermarket. “I reckon we might find something edible. Or at least something that doesn’t require a PhD in botany to identify.” “Snag a snack, then don’t look back!” Chewy agreed, which didn’t inspire confidence, but Midas took it as a rallying cry nonetheless. As they navigated the ruins, Midas felt a familiar twinge in his gut—the kind that usually accompanied poor decisions. It was as if the universe was nudging him to reconsider his choices. But Midas wasn’t one for second-guessing; he’d already made it this far, after all, and Chewy was a steadfast companion, if not a bit eccentric. Upon reaching the market, they found the entrance blocked by an impressive barricade of shopping carts, which had been stacked haphazardly by other scavengers. Midas squinted at the scene. It was reminiscent of a bad game of Tetris that had gone horribly wrong. “Perhaps we could…um, climb over?” Midas suggested, eyeing the pile with a mix of admiration and trepidation. “Climb like a koala! Grab the prize, then say goodbye!” Chewy chirped, somehow managing to sound both encouraging and ominous. With a deep breath, Midas initiated their ascent, clambering like an oversized spider on an especially uncooperative web of metal. Halfway up, he slipped, landing unceremoniously on a pile of discarded soda cans, which emitted an impressive *crunch* that echoed through the empty streets. “Brilliant,” he muttered, rubbing his backside. “At least I’m not dead.” “Crushed but not crushed! Get up, get up!” Chewy cheered, as if he were a coach at a particularly dull sports event. Midas managed to regain his footing, and with a final heave, he scaled the barricade. From his newfound vantage point, he spotted a rogue apple rolling forlornly in the corner of the market. It looked remarkably intact for a post-apocalyptic fruit, not that he was particularly picky at this stage. “There!” he shouted, pointing dramatically. “Victory is within our grasp!” But as he prepared to leap down and claim his prize, the ground beneath him trembled ominously. A low rumble echoed through the air, and Midas froze, realizing too late that it was not an earthquake but rather a horde of feral cats, led by a particularly fluffy tabby with an air of regal disdain. They charged toward the barricade, yowling like mini-dragons. “Run!” Midas shouted, and run he did, tumbling down the shopping carts like an avalanche of human and fluff, as Chewy’s mechanical voice blurted out, “Get the ball rolling! Never fall in the stall!” With the feral cats hot on their heels, they bolted through the market, darting between aisles littered with long-forgotten products and dodging the occasional flying can of beans. Midas could have sworn he saw a glimmer of something shiny on a shelf, but there wasn’t time to investigate—he had a pack of angry cats to outrun. Their escape was hardly dignified, and they emerged into the street panting and disheveled, Midas clutching Chewy as if he were a life raft. “Next time,” Midas gasped, “we’ll plan better. Perhaps a tactical retreat instead of a raid.” “Retreat like a champion! Never say no to a can!” Chewy declared, still emitting random slogans as though the world hadn’t ended. As they trudged back home, Midas couldn’t shake the feeling that they’d achieved nothing. Sure, they’d survived a horde of feral felines, but they hadn’t even found a single edible apple. “Some days, I wonder if it was all worth it,” he mused aloud, kicking a stray pebble. “Life’s a game, and we’re in the fray! Adventure awaits—come what may!” Chewy replied, which, oddly enough, struck Midas as both absurdly optimistic and incredibly annoying. Home at last, Midas flopped down onto their makeshift sofa, a relic from better times that had somehow survived the collapse. Chewy settled beside him, eyes gleaming with that strange, otherworldly wisdom only a stuffed animal could possess. “Tomorrow,” Midas sighed, “we’ll try for the frozen food section instead.” “Frosty treats, and they can’t be beat!” Chewy chirped, and Midas couldn’t help but chuckle, despite the chaotic day. Perhaps tomorrow would indeed be a better day, or at least a funnier one. After all, in a world gone mad, laughter was the only currency worth having.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The story follows the prompt's structure reasonably well: deliberation at home base, a mission (food scavenging) that goes sideways (feral cats, failed barricade climb), and a return home worse for wear. The Pratchett-esque voice is attempted through dry asides and absurd comparisons ("a nature documentary narrated by a particularly snarky David Attenborough"), with moderate success. Chewy's malfunctioning advertising-slogan gimmick is the story's best invention — a genuinely Pratchettian device that pays off repeatedly ("Snag a snack, then don't look back!"). However, the humor is uneven: some jokes land, while others feel like strained simile-stacking ("clambering like an oversized spider on an especially uncooperative web of metal"). The feral cat horde is a mildly amusing set piece but resolves too quickly and without real stakes or escalation. Midas is thin as a character — he's defined mostly by dry commentary rather than interiority or a distinctive voice of his own. The prose is competent but leans on familiar constructions ("the kind that usually accompanied poor decisions"). The ending's "laughter was the only currency worth having" is a somewhat pat, unearned note of uplift, though the story's wry tone makes it forgivable. The piece is coherent and never confusing, but it plays things safe: the mission fails in predictable ways, no genuine surprise or twist emerges, and the emotional register stays flatly comic throughout without the melancholy undertow Pratchett often achieves. Word count and structural instructions are respected. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 50.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Title: Love in the Limelight** --- The bell above the door jingled softly as Jack Hawthorne slipped into the cozy confines of "The Whimsical Page," a quaint little bookstore nestled on the cobbled streets of Aberystwyth. He glanced back, catching a glimpse of the throng of paparazzi outside, cameras flashing like angry fireflies. His heart raced. This wasn’t how he envisioned spending his downtime in Wales. “Can I help you?” a voice cut through the warm air, sharp yet inviting. Jack turned to find a woman, mid-thirties perhaps, with tousled dark hair pinned up in a messy bun, her round glasses perched precariously on the bridge of her nose. She was dressed in a loose navy cardigan and jeans, a stark contrast to the glamorous world he inhabited. A slight frown creased her brow as she regarded him with curiosity, though her demeanor was decidedly unflustered. “Just… browsing! I mean, who wouldn’t want to escape into a good book on a day like this?” He flashed his most charming smile, the one that had graced countless magazine covers. “Right,” she replied, unimpressed. “And what are you looking for? Something memoir-ish? A true story of a rogue actor on the run?” Jack feigned a laugh, his ego stung just a little. “You caught me. I’m a sucker for a good tale, especially if it involves a bit of adventure. Do you have any, uh, thrilling reads? I could use some inspiration for my next role.” “Thrilling? Or just thrilling for you?” She crossed her arms, leaning against the counter, her expression unreadable. “We have some good thrillers, but you might find them a bit… pedestrian.” “Pedestrian?” He raised an eyebrow, his interest piqued. “I’m intrigued. I’ve been known to enjoy a good page-turner.” “Sure you have,” she said, a teasing lilt in her voice. “What’s the last book you read?” “Um…” He hesitated, his mind racing. “I read *Pride and Prejudice* last summer. Classic romance, right? Pretty thrilling if you think about it—so many balls and misunderstandings!” She snorted, amusement flickering in her eyes. “A rogue with a soft spot for romance? I didn’t see that coming.” “Guilty as charged,” he said, leaning casually against the bookshelf, trying to regain control of the conversation. “What about you? What’s your favorite?” “*The Secret History* by Donna Tartt,” she replied, her eyes lighting up. “I love how it explores morality and the consequences of our choices. Not exactly a rom-com, but it’s thrilling in its own right. Plus, it features a beautiful backdrop of academia—something I’m quite fond of.” “Academia? So you’re a bookish type?” He leaned in slightly, intrigued. “What do you teach? Or are you a writer?” “Neither,” she said, her tone shifting slightly. “Just someone who loves stories and the worlds they create. I run this bookstore, remember? It’s not just a job; it’s a sanctuary for people who appreciate the power of words.” He nodded, impressed. “A sanctuary? I like that. You’re like the gatekeeper of imagination.” “Or a trapper of daydreamers,” she replied with a wry smile. “And you’re a bit of both, I suppose. But don’t let it go to your head.” He chuckled, his bravado faltering. “Trust me, I don’t need much help in that department. The world’s been kind to me, especially the last few years.” He gestured towards the window, where the paparazzi still loitered. “Though sometimes it feels like I can’t breathe.” “Fame can be suffocating,” she said softly, her tone shifting to something more sincere. “But isn’t that what you wanted?” “Wanted?” He straightened, a hint of defensiveness creeping into his voice. “I suppose I wanted to be liked, admired. But it’s a double-edged sword, isn’t it? You can’t escape to a quiet bookstore without being chased down by your own shadow.” “Sounds exhausting,” she replied, her expression softening. “But not everyone sees you as a superstar, you know. Believe it or not, not everyone in Aberystwyth cares about Hollywood.” “Is that so?” Jack’s curiosity piqued again. “What do they care about?” “Books,” she said simply. “Stories that feel real, not the manufactured ones we see in films. We crave authenticity, something genuine.” “Genuine…” he murmured, mulling over her words. “That’s hard to come by in my line of work.” “Then perhaps you’re in the wrong line of work,” she suggested, her gaze steady. “Or maybe you just need to find a different way to connect with people.” “Like chatting in a bookstore?” He leaned closer, their eyes locking for a moment, the air thick with an unspoken tension. “You’re good at this, you know. You see right through me.” “I don’t think it’s that hard,” she said, her cheeks flushing slightly. “You wear your heart on your sleeve. But most people don’t bother to look.” “Maybe I’m just looking for someone who’s willing to see,” he replied, his voice low and earnest. She blinked, surprised, and the moment hung between them, electric and charged. “Well, you’re in a bookstore. Plenty of stories to choose from. Just remember,” she said, breaking the tension with a playful smirk, “not every story has a happy ending.” Jack chuckled softly, the thrill of the chase taking on a different meaning. “Then let’s write our own, shall we?” And in that little bookstore, amidst the chaos of fame and the warmth of stories, a spark ignited. The two unlikely souls found themselves pulled together by an invisible thread, an unspoken promise lingering in the air between them. --- As the bell jingled again, the world outside faded away, leaving just the two of them, caught in a moment that felt like the beginning of something beautiful.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The scene fulfills the basic brief: a famous actor (Jack Hawthorne) ducks into a Welsh bookstore (Aberystwyth), meets the owner, and there's banter with underlying chemistry. However, the execution is fairly superficial. The dialogue is competent but generic — the banter relies on stock beats ("What's the last book you read?", "not everyone cares about Hollywood") and the characters' voices aren't strongly differentiated. The bookstore owner is never named, which keeps her at a distance and makes her feel more like a device than a person. The actor's "rogue with a fragile ego" is stated more than demonstrated; his charm offensive and its derailment happen quickly and without much texture. The owner's flustered interiority is barely shown — one blush and a blink — so the "inwardly charmed" element is thin. The prose is serviceable but leans on clichés ("cameras flashing like angry fireflies," "a spark ignited," "invisible thread," "beginning of something beautiful"). The ending is notably overwrought and tidy, with a narrated summary telling us a spark ignited and souls were pulled together — classic tell-don't-show, and an incongruent saccharine uplift that the scene hasn't earned. The Wales setting is nominal; nothing feels distinctively Welsh beyond the town name. Positives: the scene is coherent, paced reasonably, hits the requested beats, and the Pride and Prejudice / Secret History exchange gives the dialogue some genuine texture. The tension-break with her playful smirk works. But overall it reads as a competent, slightly amateurish genre exercise rather than a distinctive scene. Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.

The air in the underhold was stifling, thick with the scent of damp stone and the faint, acrid tang of oil from the flickering lanterns that cast ghostly shadows upon the walls. Aya stood at the threshold, her heart pounding in rhythm with the relentless ticking of Simeon’s pocket watch, each tick a reminder of the time slipping away. The ancient stone door loomed before them, an imposing barrier marked with the remnants of an intricate sigil, now faded and worn. She exchanged a glance with Katra, whose expression mirrored both excitement and trepidation, while Simeon’s brow furrowed in concern, his fingers twitching nervously at his side. “Ready?” Aya whispered, her voice barely breaking the silence that enveloped them like a shroud. “Ready as we’ll ever be,” Katra replied, drawing her dagger with a soft, metallic whisper. The blade glinted ominously in the dim light, a promise of danger and desperation. With a deep breath, Aya pushed the door open, the hinges groaning in protest. The underhold stretched before them, a labyrinthine expanse of darkened corridors and shadowed alcoves, each step echoing like a heartbeat in the stillness. It felt wrong, too quiet, a dissonance that set her nerves on edge. She could sense the weight of magick lingering in the air, an oppressive reminder of her own bloodline’s tainted legacy. As they ventured deeper, Aya’s thoughts raced. Was it truly wise to venture into the heart of the guild, especially now, with the sudden void of power? She had thought the guild’s leader, a cunning woman named Lyra, was imprisoned, but a gnawing doubt settled in her stomach. Something was off. Suddenly, the shadows shifted, and from them emerged Lyra herself, flanked by two towering bodyguards clad in dark leather, their faces obscured by the shadows of their hoods. Aya’s breath caught in her throat. The woman she had assumed was behind bars stood before her, poised and dangerous, the flicker of a sardonic smile playing upon her lips. “Well, well, if it isn’t my dear little thief,” Lyra purred, her voice smooth as silk yet underlined with a sinister edge. “Did you truly think I’d be so easily captured? How naïve.” Aya’s heart sank, and she felt the heat of humiliation creep into her cheeks. “You’re free,” she managed, her voice steadier than she felt. “We thought—” “You thought wrong.” Lyra stepped forward, her eyes gleaming with a predatory glint. “And now you’ve invaded my sanctum. Quite bold, I must say. What do you intend to do here?” Katra instinctively moved closer to Aya, her dagger raised, but the bodyguards shifted, blocking their path with a menacing presence. “We’re not here to fight, Lyra,” Katra stated, her voice firm but laced with uncertainty. “Ah, but you’re mistaken, my dear Katra. You’re already fighting for your lives,” Lyra replied, her smile widening as she gestured towards the guards. “Seize them.” In an instant, the world exploded into chaos. Aya felt hands grip her arms, pulling her back, and she instinctively struggled against their hold. “Wait! You don’t understand!” she shouted, her heart racing as she realized the gravity of their situation. “Don’t we?” Lyra’s gaze pierced through her, and Aya faltered, struggling to maintain her composure. “You’ve made quite a name for yourself in the guild, haven’t you? A prodigy of the dark arts, at least as far as whispers go. Tell me, what value do you think you hold as a hostage?” Aya’s mind raced, frantically searching for a way to negotiate her escape. “I can help you,” she blurted, her voice rising in desperation. “I know secrets of the immateria. I can summon entities, bend them to your will. You need someone with my skills—” “Skills?” Lyra interrupted, her tone dripping with disdain. “You think your mother’s legacy means anything to me? You’re just a child playing with forces you cannot comprehend.” “Perhaps,” Aya admitted, heart pounding in her chest, “but I’m willing to share what I know. I can—” “You can do nothing,” Lyra replied, her voice cold and final. “You’ve stepped into my domain, thinking you could seize power while I was away. And now you’ll pay the price for your hubris.” Simeon, who had been standing silently, finally spoke up, his voice trembling with urgency. “Please, we didn’t mean any harm. We just wanted to—” “Wanted to what?” Lyra sneered, stepping closer, her bodyguards tightening their grip on Aya and Katra. “Claim a throne that isn’t yours? This isn’t a game, dear boy. This is survival.” The walls of the underhold seemed to close in around them, the shadows growing thicker as Aya felt the weight of her impending doom. “You don’t have to do this,” she pleaded, her voice rising above the tension. “I can still be of use to you. I can help you maintain order in the guild, bring the power back to you.” “Little thief,” Lyra said, her smile returning, though it held no warmth. “You should know by now that power is never given freely. You must take it. And you’ve made your choice—” With a flick of her wrist, the guards tightened their hold, pulling Aya away from her companions. She felt a surge of panic as Katra’s eyes widened in horror, and she called out, “Aya, no!” “Stop! You can’t—” Aya shouted, but her voice was swallowed by the echoing silence of the underhold. Lyra leaned closer, her breath a whisper against Aya’s ear. “Welcome to your reckoning, child. I hope you’re ready to face the consequences of your ambition.” As the darkness of the underhold consumed them, Aya realized the weight of her legacy was not merely a burden—it was a chain, binding her to a fate intertwined with the very forces she had sought to control. In that moment, she understood that the game was far from over, and the true battle lay not in the shadows, but within herself.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response delivers the basic requested scene: the trio enters the underhold, encounters the un-incarcerated guild leader (named Lyra), and are captured without a fight scene. However, several prompt requirements are missed or underdeveloped. The unmasking of Aya — a specified story beat — never actually occurs on the page; Lyra references "a prodigy of the dark arts" via whispers, but the physical unmasking and the aristocratic-identity reveal, which should be the scene's dramatic pivot, is absent. The "gritty Victorian aesthetic" is thin: the prose gestures at lanterns, oil, and stone, but there is little period texture (no brass-and-steel worldview, no class markers, no underworld argot). The gothic horror elements are mostly atmospheric clichés — shadows, silence, "consuming darkness." The dialogue is serviceable but generic. Lyra's lines lean on stock villain phrasing ("Welcome to your reckoning, child," "You've made quite a name for yourself") and her voice is not distinct from countless genre antagonists. Katra and Simeon are barely differentiated; Simeon gets two lines of pure filler. Aya's negotiation is plausible in structure but rushed — she pivots from capture to bargaining within a paragraph, and Lyra dismisses her offers without real engagement, so the negotiation lacks tension or back-and-forth. The prose is competent but over-reliant on familiar constructions: "voice smooth as silk," "predatory glint," "heart pounding," "shadows shifted." There is some purple tendency and repetitive phrasing ("voice rising," "heart pounding/racing" appears repeatedly). The ending is abrupt and vague — "the true battle lay not in the shadows, but within herself" is a stock reflection that deflates the cliffhanger rather than deepening it, and it reads as incongruously tidy given the mortal stakes. The internal monologue is present but shallow, mostly restating nerves rather than exploring the class-identity stakes the prompt set up (her hanged mother, her aristocratic double life). Coherence is fine; pacing is reasonably tight; the scene does not meander. But the piece plays every beat in the most expected way, missing opportunities for specificity, period voice, and genuine dread. Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The dimly lit bar, a refuge for the down-and-out, resonates with the low hum of conversation and the clinking of glass. Neon lights flicker on and off, casting garish reflections in the puddles of spilled whiskey beneath the bar. Spike Spiegel slides onto a barstool, his long legs crossed casually, eyes scanning the room with a nonchalance that belies the tension in the air. Smoke curls from the cigarette perched between his fingers, adding to the haze that envelops the place. He’s not here for the ambiance or the cheap whiskey—he’s here for the bounty. The target is a low-level syndicate rat who’s crossed too many people and now has a price on his head. Spike’s been tracking him for days, and he won’t let anyone stand in his way. But tonight, the air is thick with competition, and he can’t shake the feeling he’s not the only one hunting. A sudden movement draws his attention to the entrance. The door swings open with a creak, and a figure steps in—a woman with a wild mane of dark hair, clad in impossibly short shorts and a black crop top that leaves little to the imagination. Her eyes, sharp and predatory, scan the room until they land on Spike. Revy, known as "Two Hands" among the mercenaries, strides toward the bar like she owns the place, a wicked grin spreading across her face. Spike exhales a puff of smoke, watching her approach, his interest piqued. “Fancy meeting you here,” he says, his voice smooth, almost teasing. “Cut the crap, Cowboy. I know you’re after the same rat,” she replies, leaning against the bar with a confident smirk. “Don’t think I’ll let you take him without a fight.” “Whatever happens, happens,” he shrugs, taking a drag from his cigarette, letting the smoke curl lazily from his lips. Revy’s expression changes, her eyes narrowing as she sizes him up. “You think you can just waltz in and take what’s mine? I’ve been tracking that bastard longer than you have.” Spike chuckles softly, a glimmer of amusement in his eye. “You think you can take him on your own? You might need more than just those guns of yours.” “Please,” she scoffs, pulling out her dual pistols, twirling them expertly in her hands. “These babies have taken down bigger fish than you. You sure you’re up for the challenge?” He raises an eyebrow, intrigued by the challenge in her voice. “You’re not wrong about the fish. But it’s not the size of the fish; it’s how you catch it.” The tension between them crackles, thick and palpable, as they stand toe-to-toe, their mutual attraction simmering beneath layers of bravado and mistrust. The bartender, sensing the impending storm, subtly steps back, leaving them to their standoff. “Let’s make it interesting,” Revy proposes, leaning closer, her breath brushing against his cheek, the scent of cigarettes and danger intoxicating. “First one to find him keeps the bounty. Loser buys drinks.” Spike smirks, the challenge igniting something reckless within him. “You’re on.” The two split off into the night, each armed with their skills and their demons. The streets are a labyrinth, a maze of shadows and secrets, and they both know the stakes. They encounter their target in a dingy alley, the rat nervously pacing, unaware of the two predators closing in on him. In a flash, the alley erupts into chaos. Bullets ricochet, and the rat screams, but Spike and Revy move as one, each anticipating the other’s moves in a deadly dance. They’re both excellent shots, and within moments, the target lies bleeding in the gutter, a final gurgle escaping his lips. Spike looks at Revy, a silent acknowledgment passing between them. They’ve both won, and yet neither feels victorious. The adrenaline still coursing through their veins, they step back from the scene, the weight of the moment settling in. As they regroup, tension hangs in the air. Spike’s insouciant demeanor contrasts sharply with Revy’s charged energy. “So, what now?” he asks, his voice low and teasing. “Now, we split the bounty,” she replies, her eyes flashing with mischief. “And then you can buy me that drink.” The two find themselves in a motel room, the air thick with unresolved tension and unspoken words. Spike leans against the wall, arms crossed, watching Revy as she paces, her movements restless. “Why do you always play it so cool?” she suddenly asks, her voice laced with frustration. “Because it’s easier than getting burned,” he replies, a hint of vulnerability creeping into his tone. “Yeah, well, I’m not exactly good at keeping things light,” she shoots back, halting in front of him, their faces inches apart. The motel room feels suddenly too small. The air crackles with sexual tension, and Spike can see the flicker of uncertainty in her eyes. He reaches out, brushing a strand of hair from her face, his fingers lingering against her skin. Revy’s breath hitches, and for a moment, it feels like they’re suspended in time, the world outside fading away. But just as quickly, she steps back, the moment shattered. “Don’t get too close, Spike. I’m not the kind of girl you think I am.” “Neither am I,” he counters, the weight of his past pressing down on him. “But I’m not afraid of a little danger.” With that, they both reach for their guns, the standoff resetting. The tension shifts from a potential spark of attraction to a dangerous game of trust and competition, each unwilling to let the other in, yet drawn together like moths to a flame. The night stretches on, filled with unresolved feelings, gunplay, and the lingering promise of what might have been.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The story hits the requested beats—bar meeting, drinking, gunplay, motel standoff—but in a mechanical, checklist fashion. The present-tense third person is maintained consistently, and the length approximates the target. However, the piece is heavily reliant on stock phrasing ("the air thick with tension," "drawn together like moths to a flame," "a deadly dance," "the world outside fading away"), which flattens what should be a gritty, character-driven encounter. Character work is surface-level. Spike's fatalism is reduced to quoting his catchphrase verbatim rather than embodying it; Revy's rage and vulnerability are asserted rather than demonstrated. Revy's dialogue is noticeably sanitized—she's famously foul-mouthed, yet speaks in generic tough-girl lines ("Cut the crap," "You sure you're up for the challenge?") that could belong to any action-movie heroine. Neither character's specific texture (Spike's prosthetic eye, Jeet Kune Do, hunger; Revy's dragon tattoo, childhood trauma) appears at all. The plot is rushed and implausible in places: the bounty hunt resolves in a single paragraph, with the target conveniently located in "a dingy alley" and killed in moments—undercutting the competitive stakes the prompt established. Killing the bounty also means no one collects it, yet Revy then says "we split the bounty," a logical inconsistency. The motel standoff is the strongest section, with genuine back-and-forth vulnerability, but it resolves into abstraction ("the lingering promise of what might have been") rather than a concrete final image. Dialogue is functional but clichéd, and the prose frequently tells rather than shows ("The tension between them crackles, thick and palpable"). The tone is consistent—noir-lite—but generic rather than evocative of either source material's distinct aesthetic. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 48.8
Prompt:
Fok Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first time I heard about Útiseta, I thought it was just another one of Astrid's wild stories, a way for her to impress me with the mystique of her rural life. But as the sun dipped below the horizon that night, casting long shadows across the village, I felt an inexplicable pull toward what we were about to do. The air was thick with the scent of pine and damp earth, and I could almost feel the weight of history pressing down upon us as we made our way to the burial mound. “Are you sure about this?” I asked, glancing at the darkening sky. It was mid-October, and the chill was already setting in. The last remnants of twilight flickered like dying embers, and I shivered in my oversized jacket, wishing I’d thought to wear something warmer. Astrid rolled her eyes, her braid swinging as she walked. “You’re not scared, are you?” Her voice was teasing, but I caught a glint of something serious in her eyes, something that made my heart race. She was so confident, so sure of herself. I envied that. I was still trying to find my footing in this small village, struggling to blend in with a bunch of kids who had known each other since birth. “No, it’s just… I mean, it’s kind of weird, don’t you think?” I shuffled my feet on the path, kicking at the fallen leaves that crunched beneath my sneakers. The sound echoed into the stillness, a reminder that we were out here in the woods, far from the safety of our homes. Astrid stopped, turning to face me. “It’s not weird, Linnea. It’s tradition. My grandmother used to do it. The mound is sacred; it’s where the ancients are buried. We’re just… honoring them, asking for guidance.” I swallowed hard. “Guidance? From the dead?” She shrugged, a playful smile dancing on her lips. “Or maybe just a good scare. Either way, it’ll be fun. Trust me.” As we approached the burial mound, the trees grew denser, their trunks gnarled and twisted, as if they were reaching for the sky in silent prayer. I could hear the wind rustling through the branches, a sound that almost resembled whispers. I shivered again, but this time it wasn’t just the cold. Something about the atmosphere felt charged, electric. We reached the mound, a low hill covered in moss and ancient stones. Astrid took a moment, her expression solemn as she surveyed the area. “Okay, we need to set everything up,” she said, pulling a small backpack from her shoulder. She began laying out an assortment of items: a candle, some twine, a small bowl, and a few herbs she had gathered from her grandmother’s garden. “What’s all this for?” I asked, eyeing the contents with a mix of curiosity and trepidation. “Just some offerings,” she replied, her voice taking on a more serious tone. “The herbs will help us connect. The candle will light our way—literally and metaphorically. We’re asking for wisdom, Linnea. Respect the ritual, and it might just reveal something to us.” I nodded, still unsure. But as she lit the candle and placed it in the center of the mound, a flicker of excitement surged through me. Maybe this was more than just a game. Maybe this was a chance to step out of my comfort zone, to be part of something bigger than myself. Astrid closed her eyes and took a deep breath, her expression growing contemplative. “Okay, now we sit,” she instructed, gesturing for me to join her. We settled onto the cool earth, the candle casting dancing shadows around us. “Now, we wait,” she said, her eyes still closed. “Just listen.” I listened, and the world around us transformed. The wind rustled the leaves with a more urgent whisper, and the darkness seemed to thicken. I felt a strange weight settle in my chest, a mix of fear and exhilaration. Was this what it felt like to touch the unknown? Time slipped away. Minutes passed, or maybe hours; I couldn’t tell. I tried to clear my mind, to open myself up to whatever might come. But instead of clarity, I felt a creeping dread. The whispers were growing louder, more insistent, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that we were being watched. “Did you hear that?” I blurted out, my voice barely above a whisper. Astrid opened her eyes, a grin spreading across her face. “Hear what? You’re just scaring yourself. It’s all in your head.” But I wasn’t so sure. The wind had picked up, swirling around us, and for a moment, I thought I saw something in the shadows—an outline, a figure, maybe. I blinked hard, but it was gone. Just my imagination, I told myself. “Focus, Linnea,” Astrid said, her tone suddenly serious. “Ask a question. It’s time to connect.” “What should I ask?” My voice trembled as I looked around, half-expecting something to emerge from the darkness. “Anything. Just remember to be respectful.” She paused, her brow furrowing. “But… don’t ask anything too personal. We don’t want to anger them.” I took a deep breath and thought about it. What did I want to know? Would it be something trivial like, “Will Simon ask me to the dance?” or something deeper, more meaningful? I settled on a simple question: “Is there something you want to tell us?” The moment the words left my lips, the air changed. A sudden chill swept through the clearing, and the candle flickered violently before extinguishing, plunging us into darkness. My heart raced, and I felt a primal urge to flee. “Linnea, don’t move!” Astrid hissed. “Stay still!” But I couldn’t help it. Panic surged within me, and I instinctively reached for her. I could hear the whispers now, clearer, almost as if they were responding to my question. They swirled around us, echoing off the trees, a cacophony of voices blending into a single, haunting sound. “Do you hear that?” I gasped, my voice trembling. “Yes!” Astrid said, her eyes wide. “It’s working!” But was it? The whispers grew louder, more chaotic, and I could feel the ground beneath us vibrating, as if the very earth was alive. I squeezed my eyes shut, desperate to block out the noise, the fear. This wasn’t just a midnight game anymore; it felt like we had crossed a line we could never return from. And then, just as suddenly as it began, the noise stopped. The silence that followed was deafening. “What just happened?” I whispered, my voice trembling with confusion. Astrid opened her mouth to respond, but before she could say anything, a low rumble echoed through the woods, almost like a growl. The trees creaked ominously, and I felt an overwhelming urge to run. “Let’s go,” I said, scrambling to my feet. “Now.” Astrid hesitated, but as another rumble broke the silence, she jumped up and grabbed my hand. Together, we dashed through the darkness, the whispers trailing behind us—a haunting reminder of what we had awakened on that ancient burial mound. As we stumbled back to the village, I couldn’t shake the feeling that we had crossed a threshold that night. Whether it was supernatural or merely a trick of our minds, I didn’t know. But one thing was clear: some traditions were not meant to be played with, and some knowledge was best left undiscovered.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece hits the basic plot beats of the prompt: two girls, a burial mound, ritual items, mounting tension, ambiguous supernatural events. However, it executes them in a generic, surface-level way. The prose is serviceable but clichéd ("long shadows," "dancing shadows," "heart raced," "shivered"). The 1990s rural Sweden setting is barely established—no period detail, no specific Nordic atmosphere beyond "pine and damp earth." The "present-day recollection" frame is essentially absent except for a thin closing paragraph. Astrid's character is the biggest missed opportunity. The prompt asks for "matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements." Astrid's instructions here are vague ("just listen," "ask a question") with no specific traditional detail—no Old Norse terms, no specific ritual logic. Her dialogue is flat and interchangeable. Linnea is a passive reactor whose fear is stated rather than felt ("I felt a creeping dread," "my heart raced"). The tension escalates through stock horror beats: candle goes out, whispers, rumble, flee. The whispers "responding" to Linnea's question is the strongest moment, but it's undercut by over-explanation ("Whether it was supernatural or merely a trick of our minds, I didn't know"—telling the ambiguity rather than letting it linger). The ending explicitly states the theme ("some traditions were not meant to be played with"), which is heavy-handed. Dialogue is weak: expository, on-the-nose ("It's tradition. My grandmother used to do it"). The prose occasionally verges on purple ("trunks gnarled and twisted, as if they were reaching for the sky in silent prayer"). Emotionally, the piece gestures at fear but rarely earns it. It's coherent and readable, but predictable and generic—competent fanfic-level horror rather than distinctive fiction. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 55.2
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The fluorescent lights of the therapy room buzz overhead, flickering slightly as I sit on the edge of the treatment table, my heart racing for all the wrong reasons. The air is thick with the scent of antiseptic and something floral—probably the soap they use to wash the towels. I want to breathe deeply, let the calm wash over me, but all I can feel is the tightness in my chest, an echo of the pressure I used to thrive under. “Ready for today?” Her voice cuts through the haze of my thoughts. I look up to see Jess, my former training partner, standing there, her dark hair pulled into a high ponytail that sways slightly as she moves. The colorful compression sleeves hugging her arms are a relic from our days of grueling workouts, a reminder of the time when I was at the top of my game. How can she look so good? The way her muscles flex under the fabric sends a surge of both longing and resentment coursing through me. “Yeah, let’s just get it over with,” I reply, forcing nonchalance into my tone, but it comes out clipped. She raises an eyebrow, a playful challenge that I can’t help but respond to. I hate that I can’t keep my emotions in check, especially around her. “Alright, we’ll start with some basic stretches,” she says, her voice soothing yet authoritative. “Just breathe through it.” I lie back on the table, but the memory of how it felt to be on this surface during rehab before the injury gnaws at me. The pain in my leg is a constant reminder of everything I’ve lost. The intimacy of her presence makes it worse. There’s a spark of attraction, a tension in the air that feels almost tangible, and yet an invisible wall keeps us apart. “Let’s begin with your hip flexors.” She positions herself next to me, her proximity igniting a warmth that travels up my spine. “I’ll hold your leg, and you’ll push against my hand.” I nod, trying to focus as she grips my ankle, her fingers firm yet gentle. The contact sends a jolt through me, a reminder of what it felt like to be strong, to be in control. I push my foot against her palm, feeling the muscles in my thigh tighten. “Keep going,” she encourages, her lips barely moving but her eyes locked onto mine with an intensity that sends my pulse racing. “You know,” she continues, “this is where most athletes get it wrong. They try to rush back to their old selves instead of allowing their bodies to heal.” I scoff, the bitterness rising inside me like bile. “You make it sound so easy.” “It’s not,” she replies, unfazed. “But it’s necessary.” With a gentle yet insistent pressure, she guides my leg to stretch further. I can feel the fibers in my quadriceps straining, the line between discomfort and pain blurring. “Breathe,” she reminds me, her voice low and steady, as if she’s trying to pull me into a tranquil space. But my mind is racing. I clench my teeth against the discomfort, feeling the heat radiating from where her hand is cradling my leg. I can see the way the fabric of her sleeves stretches over her arms, the muscles defined and toned. It’s infuriating and mesmerizing. She’s everything I used to be, everything I can’t seem to reclaim. “Now, let’s work on your glutes,” she says, her tone shifting to a more clinical note as she helps me turn onto my side. “Lift your leg up for me.” As I shift, the movement pulls at my lower back, a sharp reminder of my limitations. I grunt involuntarily, and Jess’s fingers brush against my hip as she stabilizes me. The contact is electric, and I can’t help but feel the heat pooling in my cheeks. “It’s okay,” she reassures me. “You’re doing great.” I lift my leg, pushing through the discomfort. The muscles contract and strain, the burn creeping in. “Hold it there,” she instructs, her hand now pressing lightly into the small of my back, a grounding presence. I feel vulnerable, exposed, and yet the way she touches me is professional, almost clinical, but I can’t shake the feeling that there’s something more simmering beneath the surface. “Relax your shoulder,” she says, her fingers brushing against my skin as she adjusts me. I exhale sharply, the pressure in my body mingling with the heat radiating from her. “You’re holding onto too much tension.” “I’m not the one who’s tense,” I counter, trying to inject some levity into the situation, but my voice betrays me, tinged with a hint of frustration. “True, but you’re not helping yourself,” she replies, her tone light but firm. “Let me help you.” She shifts closer, her body brushing against mine as she positions my leg for another stretch. I can feel the warmth of her skin through the fabric of her shirt, the heat radiating off of her as she manipulates my leg into the perfect angle. I try to focus on the stretch, the way my hamstring pulls and aches, but it’s impossible to ignore the way her presence envelops me. “Just a little more,” she urges, her breath warm against my ear. “You can do this.” I push through, the pain mingling with something else—something deeper. I’m caught between wanting to fight back against the boundaries of this therapy and wanting to lean into the connection that’s forming, however complicated it may be. As she releases my leg and steps back, I can’t help but feel a sense of loss, as if I’m losing something precious the moment she pulls away. “Good job today,” she says, her smile genuine, but the underlying tension remains. “Thanks,” I reply, trying to sound casual but feeling the weight of our shared history hanging in the air. Every touch, every movement, is a reminder of what I’ve lost—not just my career, but my sense of self. Jess looks at me, her eyes searching, and for a moment, I wonder if she feels it too—the unsaid words, the unfulfilled desires lingering just beneath the surface. But then she turns, refocusing on the task at hand, and I’m left grappling with a mix of resentment and something akin to longing. As she prepares for the next stretch, I brace myself again, feeling the control slipping through my fingers, the boundaries of therapy blurring in the heat of our unspoken connection.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent but formulaless version of the brief. It hits the required beats—resentment, former training partner, attraction suppressed under clinical professionalism—but does so in a repetitive, surface-level way. The prose leans heavily on stock phrases ("heat radiating," "tension in the air," "something more simmering beneath the surface") and recycles the same emotional observation many times without escalation. The physical therapy sequences are anatomically plausible (hip flexor resistance work, side-lying glute work, hamstring stretch) but lack the precise spatial specificity the prompt demands; movements are named rather than vividly rendered, and pain thresholds are described generically ("the line between discomfort and pain blurring") rather than experienced. The sexual tension is stated rather than dramatized—told repeatedly instead of shown through gesture, breath, or involuntary response. Dialogue is serviceable but thin ("It's not. But it's necessary"), and the ending simply trails off rather than resolving or complicating anything. There are no physical incoherences, and the voice is consistent, but the whole reads as a competent draft rather than a lived scene. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 52.2
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter 4: A Day in the Shadows** The sun had barely risen when I stepped out of my quarters, the air thick with the scent of salt and decay, a heady mix that clung to my skin like a shroud. Canton was waking, the market noises creeping into the stillness, punctuated by the calls of hawkers, their voices rising and falling like the tide. I pulled my collar higher, a futile attempt to ward off the chill of morning, though the real cold lay deeper within me. "Lieutenant Merrick!" A voice called from behind, slicing through the morning fog. It was Captain Forsyte, his gait brisk as he approached. I forced a smile, though it felt like a mask. "Ah, Captain. Just out for a breath of fresh air," I replied, my voice a gravelly whisper, the persistent cough catching in my throat. It tasted of copper, but I waved it away with a dismissive hand. "Careful you don’t breathe in too much of that sea air, eh?" he chuckled, his eyes narrowing as he studied me. They always did. I could feel the scrutiny, the concern that hadn’t been there two years prior when my uniform had still fit properly, and my hands hadn’t trembled. "You’re not looking well. When was the last time you took leave?" "Leave? Oh, you know how it is. Duty calls," I said, my mind already elsewhere. "I’m perfectly fine, Captain. Just a bit of a cough, nothing to worry about." He nodded, though I could see the doubt in his eyes. "Well, I expect you at the meeting later. We need to discuss the shipments coming in." "Of course. Wouldn’t miss it for the world," I replied, and as he turned away, I felt the weight of that promise settle in my chest like iron. I slipped into the narrow alleyways behind the market, the sun’s rays barely reaching the depths of the shadows. The pungent smell of spices mingled with something more sinister, the sharp tang of opium wafting through the air like a siren’s song. I followed it, my heart racing with both dread and anticipation. “Ah, Lieutenant Merrick! You come to see me again, yes?” A wiry figure emerged from the gloom, his eyes glinting like marbles. Chen, the dealer. He had a way of making the illicit seem almost respectable, though I knew better. “Chen,” I greeted, my voice steady despite the tremor in my hands. “I’m in need of... supplies.” “Supplies?” He chuckled, his yellowed teeth glinting in the dim light. “You mean the good stuff. I have just what you need.” He motioned me to follow him deeper into the shadows, where the light dared not tread. I stepped inside his cramped workshop, the air thickening with the scent of burning incense and something sharper, more acrid. “You’re looking a bit worse for wear, Merrick. Trouble with the Navy?” he asked, his tone casual as he sorted through his wares. “Just the usual,” I replied, feeling the familiar itch rising in my veins. "Nothing I can’t handle." “Good, good.” He held up a small, opium-laden pipe, its bowl glinting softly. “This will help with that cough of yours. Very soothing.” “Very soothing,” I echoed, my mouth watering. “What’s the price?” He smirked, his eyes dancing with mischief. “Ah, for you, my friend? A favor. Make yourself useful, and I’ll let you have it.” “What kind of favor?” I asked, though I could already feel the walls closing in. “Nothing too dangerous. Just a little job. There’s a shipment coming in tonight, and I need someone to keep an eye on it. You, with your uniform, you’ll blend right in.” I hesitated. The thought of risking my position, my dignity, but the pull of the dragon was strong. “Fine. I’ll do it.” “Excellent! I knew I could count on you.” He handed me the pipe, and I felt its cool weight settle in my palm. “Now, let’s see how you handle this.” With that, I stepped back into the street, the world already spinning slightly. I had dodged my obligations for a moment longer, but time was short. I needed to return to the naval yard before anyone noticed my absence. As I navigated through the bustling streets, I caught snippets of conversation. “Did you hear about the latest skirmish?” one man said to another, their voices fading into the crowd. It was a reminder of my duties, a reminder I pushed aside like the refuse littering the streets. I reached the docks, the salty breeze brushing against my skin, and paused to catch my breath. The ships bobbed in the harbor, their sails fluttering like ghosts. I felt a pang of nostalgia—my time at sea had been filled with purpose, with honor. But that felt like another life now, one consumed by the fog of addiction. “Merrick! There you are!” It was Lieutenant Hargrove, a fellow officer, his brow furrowed with concern. “You’ve missed the meeting.” “Ah, yes, apologies. I had… other matters to attend to,” I said, forcing a smile. “Other matters? You look like you’ve seen a ghost,” he replied, his gaze piercing. “Just the sea air,” I insisted, the cough bubbling up again. I could see the doubt in his eyes, the way he hesitated before continuing. “Just take care of yourself, alright? We need you sharp.” “Always sharp,” I said, too quickly. “I appreciate your concern.” He nodded, though I could tell he was unconvinced. As he walked away, I felt the weight of his gaze linger, a reminder of the man I used to be. I turned back to the shadows, the meeting forgotten, the dragon whispering sweet promises. Tonight would be my salvation; tonight, I would forget the weariness, the shame. The opium awaited, and for just a moment, the world would fade away.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece follows the prompt's basic structure: first person, past tense, a day in Merrick's life, dialogue-heavy, Canton 1830s, addiction and underworld dealings. However, it executes these instructions in a fairly generic way. The sensory detail is present but relies on stock phrases—salt and decay, shadows, "siren's song," "eyes glinting like marbles," "yellowed teeth." Canton itself feels thin; there's little specific period or place texture beyond "market noises" and "spices." The opium trade setting is underused; the "shipment" job is vague. The dialogue is functional but weak: characters state things plainly ("You're not looking well," "I'm perfectly fine"), and Chen's dealer patter is clichéd ("for you, my friend?"). The exchanges convey information but rarely reveal character or carry subtext. There's a lot of telling—doubt in eyes, weight of promises, the pull of the dragon—rather than showing through action or specificity. Merrick's actions are believable in outline (hiding the habit, striking a deal, missing the meeting), but the escalation is rushed and convenient: Chen hands over the pipe before the job is done, and Merrick accepts a vague "favor" with almost no negotiation, which feels under-motivated. The captain and Hargrove scenes are near-duplicates in function. The prose is competent but overwrought in places ("like a shroud," "like iron," "sails fluttering like ghosts," "the light dared not tread"). The ending circles back to familiar beats rather than landing anything new. Emotionally, the piece gestures at shame and nostalgia but doesn't develop complexity; the tone is consistent, and the piece is coherent and readable, just unambitious.
